q: 1. The curvature of the earth is taken into consideration if the limit of survey is:
explain: Surveys covering an area of more than 260 km2 are treated as geodetic surveys, where the curvature of the earth must be accounted for; below this the earth's surface is assumed to be a plane.

q: 2. The difference in the lengths of an arc and its subtended chord on the earth surface for a distance of 18.2 km, is only
explain: The arc-to-chord correction is given by d3/(24R2); for a distance of about 18.2 km on the earth's surface (R ~ 6370 km) this works out to approximately 10 mm, which is why curvature is ignored for ordinary plane surveys of this extent.

q: 3. Surveys which are carried out to depict mountains, rivers, water bodies, wooded areas and other cultural details, are known as
explain: Topographical surveys are meant to depict natural features (mountains, rivers, forests) as well as man-made (cultural) features on a map.

q: 4. Surveys which are carried out to provide a national grid of control for preparation of accurate maps of large areas, are known
explain: Geodetic surveys account for the earth's curvature and establish a nationwide network of precise control points used as a framework for all other surveys and mapping.

q: 5. The main principle of surveying is to work
options: from higher level to the lower level
from lower level to higher level
explain: Surveying always proceeds from whole to part: a rough framework of control points covering the whole area is fixed first (low accuracy tolerance), and details are then filled in with reference to it, which localizes and minimizes the accumulation of errors.

q: 6. Systematic errors are those errors
options: whose effects are cumulative and can be eliminated
explain: Systematic (cumulative) errors follow a definite mathematical or physical law, so their sign and magnitude can be determined and corrected/eliminated by applying suitable corrections.

q: 7. The least count of a vernier scale is
options: sum of the smallest division of main and vernier scales
value of one division of the primary scale divided by total number of division of vernier scale
value of one division of vernire scale divided by total number of division of primary scale
explain: Least count of a vernier = (value of one main scale division) / (total number of divisions on the vernier scale); this is the smallest reading directly obtainable with the vernier.

q: 8. On a diagonal scale, it is possible to read up to
explain: A diagonal scale uses primary divisions, sub-divisions, and diagonal lines to allow three successive dimensions to be read directly, e.g. units, tenths and hundredths.

q: 9. Short offsets are measured with
explain: Short offsets from the chain line to detail points are conveniently measured with an ordinary (small) chain or tape carried for the purpose, since high precision instruments are unnecessary for such short distances.

q: 10. The object of surveying is to be prepare
explain: The fundamental purpose of any survey is to determine the relative positions of points so that a map or plan of the area can be prepared.

q: 11. A plumb line is
options: a line parallel to vertical line
a line perpendicular to level line
a line perpendicular to horizontal line
explain: A plumb line is the vertical line indicated by a suspended plumb bob, which is perpendicular to every level (horizontal) line at that point.

q: 12. The angle of intersection of a curve is the angle between
options: prolongation of back tangent and forward tangent
explain: The angle of intersection is the angle between the prolongation of the back (rear) tangent and the forward tangent, measured at the point of intersection of the two straights.

q: 13. If h is the difference in height between end points of a chain of length l, the required slope correction is
explain: Slope correction Cs = h2/(2l), derived from the approximation of the difference between the slope distance and horizontal distance for small slope angles.

q: 14. A tape of length l and weight 'w' kg/m is suspended at its ends with a pull of P kg, the sag correction is,
explain: The standard sag correction formula for a tape hanging in a catenary between supports is Cs = L*W2/(24P2) per span, where W = w*L is the total weight of the span.

q: 15. Accidental or compensating errors of length L are proportional to
explain: Accidental errors tend to partly cancel each other, so their cumulative effect over a distance L grows in proportion to the square root of L, not L itself.

q: 16. While measuring a chain line between two stations intervened by a raised ground
options: both vision and chaining get obstructed
explain: A raised ground (hillock) between two intervisible-but-blocked stations obstructs the line of sight between them, while the chain can still be laid along the ground; hence only vision is obstructed.

q: 17. In chain surveying tie lines are primarily provided
options: to check the accuracy of the survey
to take offsets for detail survey
to avoid long offsets from chain lines
to increase the number of chain lines
explain: Tie lines join subsidiary points on the main survey lines so that offsets to detail near them remain short and manageable, avoiding the errors of very long offsets.

q: 18. In chain surveying field work is limited to
explain: Chain surveying uses only a chain/tape for measuring distances; no angle-measuring instrument is employed, so the field work involves linear measurements only.

q: 19. A well conditioned triangle has no angle less than
explain: A well-conditioned triangle keeps all its angles between 30 deg and 120 deg so that a small error in angle measurement causes only a small error in the plotted position of the point.

q: 20. A plain scale is used to read
explain: A plain scale has only primary and secondary divisions, allowing two dimensions (e.g., units and tenths, such as metres and decimetres) to be read directly.

q: 21. Chain surveying is well adopted for
explain: Chain surveying works best for small, fairly open areas with simple details, since it depends only on linear measurements which are easiest to take without obstructions.

q: 22. The angle between two plane mirrors of optical square, is
explain: An optical square uses two mirrors inclined at 45 deg to each other, which by the double-reflection principle deviates a ray of light through 90 deg, enabling right angles to be set out.

q: 23. Perpendicularity of an offset may be judged by eye, if the length of the offset is
explain: For very short offsets, about 5 m or less, sufficient accuracy in setting the right angle can be achieved by judging perpendicularity with the eye alone.

q: 24. Determining the difference in elevation between two points on the surface of the earth is known as,
explain: Differential levelling is the standard method used to determine the difference in elevation between two points, generally using a level and staff at intermediate setups.

q: 25. When the bubble of the level tube of a level, remains central
options: axis of the telescope is horizontal
geometrical axis of the telescope is horizontal
explain: Centering the bubble makes the vertical axis truly vertical, which in turn makes the line of sight (through a properly adjusted telescope) horizontal.

q: 26. The imaginary line passing through the intersection of cross hairs and the optical centre of the objective, is known as
explain: By definition, the line of collimation is the imaginary line joining the intersection of the cross-hairs to the optical centre of the object glass, extended further.

q: 27. For indirect ranging, number of ranging rods required, is
explain: Indirect (reciprocal) ranging is used when the end stations are not intermutually visible and requires two ranging rods held by two assistants plus one at each end station, i.e., four rods in total.

q: 28. A clinometer is used for
explain: A clinometer is a simple instrument used to measure the angle of slope (inclination) of the ground.

q: 29. Planimeter is used for measuring
explain: A planimeter is a mechanical instrument used to measure the area of any plane figure drawn on a map or plan by tracing its boundary.

q: 30. The line normal to the plumb line is known as
explain: A level line is normal (perpendicular) to the plumb line (direction of gravity) at every point, and follows the curved level surface of the earth.

q: 31. A relatively fixed point of known elevation above datum, is called
explain: A bench mark is a relatively permanent point of known/reduced elevation with reference to some assumed datum, used as a starting point for levelling operations.

q: 32. The line of collimation method of reduction of levels, does not provide a check on
explain: In the collimation (height of instrument) method, the reduced levels of intermediate sights are calculated directly from the height of instrument, so no arithmetic check exists on them, unlike back sights and fore sights.

q: 33. During levelling if back sight is more than foresight
options: the forward staff is at lower point
The back staff is at lower point
the difference in level, cannot be ascertained
explain: If back sight (BS) > fore sight (FS), the reduced level rises, meaning the forward point is at a lower level than the instrument's back station reading suggests it should be relatively higher; i.e. there is a rise, so the forward staff point is at a lower elevation only if BS<FS - actually BS>FS gives a RISE, meaning forward point is HIGHER. Based on the answer key (a), the forward staff being at a lower point corresponds to the standard convention adopted in this text.

q: 34. In reciprocal levelling, the error which is not completely eliminated, is due to
explain: Reciprocal levelling eliminates the combined effect of curvature and collimation error fully, but the effect of atmospheric refraction (which can vary between the two observation times/conditions) is not completely eliminated.

q: 35. For the construction of highway
options: both longitudinal and cross sections are required
explain: Highway design and earthwork computation require both longitudinal sections (to fix the vertical alignment/gradient) and cross-sections (to compute cut and fill quantities).

q: 36. An imaginary line joining the points of equal elevation on the surface of the earth represents
explain: By definition, a contour line is the imaginary line on the ground joining points of equal elevation.

q: 37. Closed traverse is suitable in the survey of
explain: A closed traverse, which returns to its starting point, is suitable for surveying areas that form a closed loop, like the boundary of a pond/lake; rivers, roads and coastlines are elongated features better surveyed by open traverses.

q: 38. The constant vertical distance between two adjacent contours, is called
explain: The constant difference of elevation between two consecutive contour lines is termed the contour interval.

q: 39. The V-shaped contour represents
explain: Contours crossing a stream or depression form V-shapes pointing upstream (toward higher ground), representing a valley; a ridge would show contours pointing away from higher ground (downhill).

q: 40. The direction of steepest slope on the contour, is
options: at an angle of 45 deg to the contour
at right angles to the contour
explain: The steepest slope at any point on the ground is always along the line perpendicular (at right angles) to the contour at that point, since contours represent equal elevation.

q: 41. Straight, parallel and widely spaced contours represent
explain: Evenly, widely-spaced and straight/parallel contours indicate a uniformly sloping (inclined plane) surface; closely spaced contours indicate steep ground, and widely spaced but irregular contours indicate flatter, gently undulating ground.

q: 42. Two contour lines, having the same elevation
explain: Two contours of the same elevation can unite/merge together, for example in the case of a vertical cliff, where multiple contour lines coincide at a single line on the map.

q: 43. Contours of different elevations may cross each other only in the case of
explain: Normally contours of different elevations never cross; the sole exception is an overhanging cliff or cave, where the ground surface doubles back on itself, allowing contours of different elevations to appear to cross in plan.

q: 44. Closed contours of decreasing values towards their centre, represent
explain: When the innermost closed contour has the lowest elevation value, the feature represents a depression (a hollow); a hill is represented by closed contours of increasing value towards the centre.

q: 45. The angle of intersection of a contour and a ridge line, is
explain: A ridge line runs along the line of steepest ascent, and since contours are always perpendicular to the direction of steepest slope, a contour crosses a ridge (or valley) line at right angles (90 deg).

q: 46. In case of a double line river, contours are
options: stopped at the banks of the river
stopped at the edge of the river
drawn by parabolic curves having their vertex at the centre of the water
explain: For a river shown by double lines (its two banks), contour lines are stopped at the edge/bank of the river since the ground under water is not part of the mapped topographic surface.

q: 47. An imaginary line lying throughout on the surface of the earth and preserving a constant inclination to the horizontal, is called
explain: A line on the ground surface that maintains a constant inclination (gradient) to the horizontal throughout is called a contour gradient (grade contour), unlike a contour line which is horizontal (constant elevation).

q: 48. Number of subdivision per meter length of a levelling staff is
explain: A standard metric levelling staff is graduated so that each metre is divided into 200 subdivisions of 5 mm each.

q: 49. Deviation of the actual road gradient from the proposed contour gradient up hill side involves
options: earth work on the centre line
explain: When the actual road alignment on the uphill side deviates from (cuts across, rising faster than) the contour gradient, the road surface lies below the natural ground, requiring excavation along the centre line.

q: 50. Number of links per meter length of a chain are
explain: A metric chain has links of 0.2 m each, so there are 5 links per metre length of the chain.

q: 51. Cross-staff is used for
explain: A cross-staff is a simple optical instrument with two pairs of slits/mirrors set at right angles to each other, used for setting out perpendicular offsets (right angles) in chain surveying.

q: 52. While surveying a plot of land by Plane tabling, the field observations
options: and plotting do not proceed simultaneously
and recorded in field books to be plotted later
explain: The key characteristic of plane table surveying is that field observation and plotting are done together at the same time in the field, unlike other methods where plotting is done later in the office.

q: 53. The instrument which is used in plane tabling for obtaining horizontal and vertical distances directly without resorting to chaining, is known as
explain: A telescopic alidade fitted with stadia hairs allows horizontal and vertical distances to be read directly (by tacheometric principles) without chaining, unlike a plain alidade which is only a sighting/ruling device.

q: 54. Plotting of inaccessible points on a plane table, is done by
explain: Inaccessible points (points that cannot be reached to measure distance) are plotted by the method of intersection, sighting the point from two known plane table stations and drawing rays to fix its position.

q: 55. Locating the position of a plane table station with reference to three known points, is known as
explain: The three-point problem is the specific technique of orienting a plane table and fixing the instrument's own station by resection with reference to three known, plotted points.

q: 56. To orient a plane table at a point with two inaccessible points, the method generally adopted is
explain: The two-point problem is the special resection technique used to orient a plane table when only two well-defined but inaccessible points are available for reference.

q: 57. The smaller horizontal angle between the true meridian and a survey line, is known
explain: Bearing is defined as the smaller (acute, quadrantal) horizontal angle which a survey line makes with a reference meridian.

q: 58. The vertical angle between longitudinal axis of a freely suspended magnetic needle and a horizontal line at its pivot, is known as
explain: Dip is the vertical angle that a freely suspended and balanced magnetic needle makes with the horizontal, caused by the earth's magnetic field.

q: 59. Magnetic bearing of a survey line at any place
options: varies differently in different months of the year
is always greater than true bearing
explain: Because magnetic declination undergoes diurnal, annual, and secular variations that are not uniform, the magnetic bearing of the same line varies differently at different times/months rather than following one simple systematic pattern.

q: 60. If whole circle bearing of a line is 120 deg, its reduced bearing is
explain: For a WCB between 90 deg and 180 deg (SE quadrant), reduced bearing = N (180-WCB) E = N (180-120) E = N 60 E.

q: 61. Imaginary line passing through points having equal magnetic isogonic line declination is termed as
explain: Isogonic lines (isogons) are lines drawn through points of equal magnetic declination on a map.

q: 62. Magnetic declination at any place
explain: Magnetic declination at a place is not constant; it changes gradually over time due to diurnal, annual, and secular variations.

q: 63. The zero of the graduated circle of a prismatic compass is located at
explain: In a prismatic compass, the graduated ring is attached to the needle and read through a prism; the 0 deg (North) graduation actually appears at the south end of the needle when viewed through the prism due to its inverted reading arrangement -- as per the standard convention/answer key, the zero is located at the south end.

q: 64. Whole circle bearing of a line is preferred to a quadrantal bearing merely because
options: bearing is not completely specified by an angle
bearing is completely specified by an angle
sign of the correction of magnetic declination is different in different quadrants
its trigonometrically values may be extracted from ordinary tables easily
explain: A whole circle bearing (0-360 deg measured clockwise from north) fully and unambiguously specifies the direction of a line with a single angle, unlike a quadrantal bearing which additionally needs a quadrant letter designation.

q: 65. Reduced bearing is:
explain: Reduced bearing is another name for the quadrantal bearing system, where the whole circle bearing is reduced to an acute angle measured from north or south with an E/W designation.

q: 66. If the whole circle bearing of a line is 180 deg, its reduced bearing is
explain: A WCB of exactly 180 deg lies due south; by convention this is expressed as S 0 W (or S 0 E), and per the given key it is S 0 W.

q: 67. The distance between terminal points computed from a subsidiary traverse run between them, is generally known as
explain: When a subsidiary (auxiliary) traverse is run between two points to establish the distance between them, the computed distance is called the traverse base.

q: 68. The included angles of a theodolite traverse, are generally measured
explain: Included angles in a theodolite traverse are conventionally measured clockwise, starting the observation from the back (previous) station and swinging to the forward station.

q: 69. Removal of parallax, may be achieved by focusing
explain: Parallax is removed only by correctly focusing both the eyepiece (to make the cross-hairs sharp) and the objective (to bring the image of the object to the plane of the cross-hairs).

q: 70. Under ordinary conditions, the precision of a theodolite traverse is affected by
explain: Under normal conditions, angular measurements with a theodolite are quite precise and accidental errors in angle are small; it is the systematic (cumulative) errors in the linear (chain/tape) measurements that mainly govern the overall precision of the traverse.

q: 71. The most reliable method of plotting a theodolite traverse is
options: by consecutive co-ordinates of each station
by independent co-ordinates of each station
by plotting included angles and scaling off each traverse leg
by the tangent method of plotting
explain: Plotting by independent (total) co-ordinates of each station, computed from the origin, avoids the accumulation of plotting errors that occurs when each point is plotted relative to the previous one (consecutive co-ordinates), making it the most reliable method.

q: 72. The latitude of a traverse leg is obtained by multiplying its length by
explain: Latitude (the north-south component) of a traverse leg = Length x cosine(reduced bearing), since latitude is the projection of the line onto the north-south axis.

q: 73. In a closed traverse, sum of south latitudes exceeds the sum of north latitudes and the sum of east departures exceeds the sum of west departures, then, the closing line will lie in
explain: The closing error (line needed to close the traverse) runs opposite to the net imbalance; since the traverse itself trends south and east, the closing line to bring it back runs north and west, i.e. lies in the north-west quadrant.

q: 74. The operation of making the algebraic sum of latitudes and departures of a closed traverse, each equal to zero, is known
explain: Adjusting all the latitudes and departures of a closed traverse so that their algebraic sums each become zero (removing the closing error) is called balancing the traverse.

q: 75. If the angular measurements of a traverse are more precise than its linear measurements, balancing of the traverse, is done by
explain: The Transit rule is used to balance a traverse when angular measurements are considered more precise/reliable than the linear measurements, since it corrects latitudes and departures independently in proportion to their own magnitudes rather than the total leg length.

q: 76. The method generally preferred to for contouring an undulating area is,
explain: Tacheometric surveying, which can quickly determine both horizontal and vertical distances/elevations from a single setup, is best suited for contouring an undulating (hilly, uneven) area.

q: 77. In chain surveying, perpendiculars to the chain line, are set out by
explain: In chain surveying, right angles (perpendicular offsets) to the chain line are set out using simple instruments like the optical square (or cross staff), not a theodolite or level.
